The 1980 atlas
Wednesday, 30 December, in the haulage company's car park. Costel is getting his truck ready for his first trip to Valencia, on 11 January. Mr Dan and Ana are helping him.
Costel, why are you taking that old atlas? The truck has GPS.
Don Andrés gave it to me. I'm taking it so that it keeps me company. And just in case, in case the GPS fails in the Pyrenees.
The roads of 1980 aren't today's roads. Many have changed, so don't rely on it too much.
I know. But don Andrés underlined the route from Madrid to Valencia in pencil. I want to follow it at least once.
Then I'll put the addresses in your phone, so that you have both: the atlas and the GPS.
And I've made you a table of rest areas, so that you don't drive more than four hours in a row.
I'm so nervous that I haven't slept for two nights.
It's your first long trip in years; hence the nerves. It's normal.
So tonight you sleep. That's an engineer's order.
Yes, sir. But first, grapes. Tomorrow is New Year's Eve and Marta says you have to eat twelve.

The subjunctive tense follows the main verb: «Te lo doy para que lo leas» (present), «Te lo di para que lo leyeras» (past).
2. Precaution: no sea que, no vaya a ser que
Take your coat, in case it's cold.
He closed the window, in case the snow came in.
Speak quietly, so you don't wake the baby.
"No sea que" and "no vaya a ser que" are very colloquial and usually come after a piece of advice or a precautionary action.
3. De modo que: purpose or consequence?
de modo que / de manera que + subj.
PURPOSE (so that)
Habló despacio de modo que todos lo entendieran.
de modo que / de manera que + ind.
CONSEQUENCE (so)
Habló despacio, de modo que todos lo entendieron.
así que + ind.
consequence (colloquial)
Estaba cansado, así que se fue a dormir.
por lo tanto / por consiguiente
consequence (formal)
Las carreteras han cambiado; por lo tanto, no te fíes.
Consequence is usually separated by a comma: «Habló despacio, de modo que lo entendieron». Purpose is not: «Habló despacio de modo que lo entendieran».
4. Intensity and known consequence
tan + adj./adv. + que
Estaba tan nervioso que no durmió.
He was so nervous that he didn't sleep.
tanto/a/os/as + noun + que
Había tanta nieve que no pudieron salir.
There was so much snow that they couldn't go out.
verb + tanto que
Nevó tanto que se cerró la carretera.
It snowed so much that the road was closed.
de ahí que + subj.
Era su primer viaje; de ahí que estuviera nervioso.
It was his first trip; hence his nerves.
"De ahí que" takes the subjunctive even when it refers to a real fact, because the fact is already known: you don't announce it, you explain it.

Diciembre

Ecaterina spent the first week of December writing letters. Not emails, but real letters, by hand, one by one, to each of the four hundred and twelve people who had written to the newspaper. She explained that she was preparing a book with some of those letters, so that other people would dare to send theirs, and asked their permission to publish their own. She offered to change the names, so that nobody could recognise them. And she told them that if they didn't want to, that was fine: their letter would go back to the drawer it had come from, which was also a good place. She wrote forty a day. At the end of each afternoon her wrist hurt so much that she had to put it in cold water.

Ana told her she could print them, that nobody would be offended. Ecaterina answered no, that those people had written to her by hand, and that therefore she had to reply by hand. That it was a question of courtesy, but also of fairness. Her right wrist, the one she had broken in March on the ice outside the post office, complained every evening, which is why Ecaterina started writing the addresses on the envelopes with her left hand. It came out crooked and shaky, like Rosa Elena's. Ana told her it looked like a five-year-old's handwriting. Ecaterina replied that this was exactly what she was aiming for, in case anyone took her too seriously.

The replies began to arrive in mid-December. The first was from the woman in Valencia, the one with letter number two hundred, who had slipped the letter into her daughter's handbag. She said yes, that she could publish it with her real name, because she no longer had anything to hide. Then came the one from Joaquín, from Zaragoza, the one with the brother. He said yes, and added a postscript: he and his brother had spent the Constitution Day long weekend together, for the first time in thirty years, and had raised a glass to her. By Christmas Eve, Ecaterina had two hundred and thirty replies. Two hundred and twenty-eight said yes. Two said no, very politely, and thanked her for asking.

Ecaterina put those two letters in a separate envelope, very carefully, and never opened them again. She told Ana that those two "no"s seemed as precious to her as the two hundred and twenty-eight "yes"es, because they proved that people had really read her letter and had decided freely. Ana asked her what she would do with them. Ecaterina answered nothing, that she would keep them in the third drawer of the desk, the one that had been empty for so long and now held the copy of doña Remedios's bookmark. She said a drawer with two letters that didn't want to be read was the best place in the world for them to stay unread.

That same week, Ecaterina also wrote to Triana. She told doña Remedios that she planned to write the anthology's introduction in February, and asked whether the room upstairs was still free. Doña Remedios replied by return of post, in her large, round handwriting. She wrote that the room was hers, that she didn't need to ask, and that she had already put a new table in front of the window, so that she could see the orange tree while she wrote. Faustino had added a line at the end: he had put all the bookshop's Neruda books on the shelf, so that she wouldn't lack inspiration, and had hidden the Machado ones, in case she got distracted.

At Rosa Elena's school, the Friday Spanish club had grown so much that Mrs Ionescu had had to ask for a bigger classroom. There were no longer six children but fourteen, plus two mothers who came secretly and sat at the back with a notebook. For the Christmas show, the head teacher asked them to prepare something in Spanish, so that the parents could see what they had learned. Rosa Elena suggested a carol. Mrs Ionescu suggested "Los peces en el río", because it was the only one she knew. Rosa Elena agreed, but on one condition: there had to be a lit lamp on the stage. The teacher asked her what for. Rosa Elena answered: so that everything could be seen properly.

They rehearsed for three weeks. Rosa Elena took charge of pronunciation, with a severity that frightened her classmates. She corrected the strong "r" in "río" until it came out like a motorbike, and explained that the "j" in "Jesús" had to be said as if you were fogging up a window with your breath. To a boy called Tudor, who couldn't manage to say "beben", she said to think of it as "bebé" plus "n". It worked. Mrs Ionescu told Ana that Rosa Elena had invented a pronunciation method that wasn't in any book, and that it was so effective she was using it herself to correct her own pronunciation, secretly, in the evenings.

The show was on Thursday, 17 December, in the school gym, decorated with paper garlands. Ana and Mihai came, Grandma Elena, Ecaterina, Mr Dan and his wife, Mrs Florica and her husband, and Costel, who had swapped a shift again. When it was the Spanish club's turn, Mrs Ionescu switched off the gym lights, so that only the toy lamp Rosa Elena had placed in the middle of the stage stayed lit. The fourteen children sang "Los peces en el río" with almost perfect pronunciation. Tudor said "beben" without a single mistake. When they finished, there was such a long silence that the head teacher thought nobody had liked it.

Then the applause burst out. Ecaterina was clapping with her eyes full of tears, and Mr Dan, beside her, was blowing his nose very loudly to hide it. Rosa Elena stepped forward, bowed like an actress and said, in Spanish, a sentence that wasn't in the programme: "This song is for Grandpa Gheorghe, who couldn't come because it's snowing a lot, so that he can hear it from the village." Mihai, who was filming everything on his phone, sent it to Grandpa that same night. Elena told them later that Grandpa had watched it eleven times in a row, with the oil lamp lit beside him, and that the eleventh time he had started singing along.

On the way out of the gym, Mrs Ionescu came up to Ecaterina. She told her that Rosa Elena had talked so much about her that the club children thought she was a character from a fairy tale, and asked whether she could come one Friday in January to talk to them about her work, so that they could see that translators really existed. Ecaterina agreed, but on one condition: that Rosa Elena introduce her. The teacher laughed and told her that had already been decided, that the girl had been preparing her speech for a month. Ecaterina asked how long it was. Mrs Ionescu answered that the last time she had rehearsed it in front of her, it had lasted twenty-two minutes.

Costel, meanwhile, was preparing his first trip to Valencia as if it were an expedition to the North Pole. He was leaving on Monday, 11 January, at five in the morning, with a truck loaded with furniture, and had to arrive on Thursday afternoon. He had checked the truck three times with the company mechanic, so that there would be no surprises in the Pyrenees. He had bought snow chains, although he was told he wouldn't need them on the motorway. And he had taken out of his wardrobe something he had kept in a plastic bag for almost two years: the 1980 road atlas of Spain that don Andrés had given him.

Don Andrés had given it to him in the spring of his last year, in Madrid, one afternoon when Costel had gone to visit him with Ecaterina. He had told him it was the atlas with which he had travelled around Spain as a young man, selling books in the villages to pay for his studies, and that a trucker would appreciate it more than anyone. Costel opened it properly for the first time that week in December, on the kitchen table. The pages smelled of old paper and tobacco. And on the page with Castilla-La Mancha and the Valencian Community he discovered something he had never seen: a very fine pencil line linking Madrid and Valencia along roads that no longer existed.

Next to the line, in the margin, there was a date written in don Andrés's small, cramped handwriting: "July 1979". And underneath, three words: "With E. Sea." Costel looked at those words for a long time. Then he called Ecaterina and read them to her over the phone. Ecaterina said nothing for a while. Then she explained, in a very faint voice, that in July 1979 she and Andrés had driven a borrowed car from Madrid to Valencia, to see the sea, because she had never seen it. That it had taken them seven hours, on mountain roads, and that it had been the happiest journey of her life. That she hadn't known he had written it down.

Costel promised her he would drive that route. Not all of it, because with a forty-tonne truck it was impossible to get onto some of those mountain roads, but at least a stretch, the last one, the one that went down to the sea. When Mr Dan found out, he spent two nights comparing the 1980 atlas with current maps, in order to find the exact stretch that could still be driven by truck. He found it: twenty-three kilometres of national road, between the mountains and the coast, which had stayed the same as in 1979. He marked it on Costel's GPS with a red flag, so that he wouldn't miss it. And he told him to drive it slowly, so that he would have time to look.

That evening, Costel had a video call with his daughter and Álex. He told Álex about Grandpa Gheorghe's walnuts and said he would bring them on his first trip, so that he could plant one. Álex asked him where, because they lived in a seventh-floor flat with no garden, and the balcony was so small that not even a chair fitted on it. Costel hadn't thought of that. His daughter, who was listening to everything, said that Álex's school had a school garden, so the problem was solved. Álex said that then the walnut tree would take ten years to produce walnuts, and by then he would be twenty-five. Costel answered: precisely.

Andrei arrived in Bucharest on 21 December, on the last flight of the night. This time he wasn't alone: Marta came with him, with the proofs of "La librera de Triana" in her suitcase, because Inés wanted the corrections before 7 January, and Marta had said she intended to correct them in Bucharest, in case she spent the holidays alone in Madrid staring at the ceiling. Mr Dan and his wife were waiting for them at the airport. Mr Dan hugged his son for so long that people started to look at them. Then he asked him how you said "I've missed you" in Spanish. Andrei told him he already knew that. His father replied that he wanted to hear him say it.

At home that evening, Andrei discovered that his father had changed. He no longer made tables. He checked his email every hour, in case the C1 results came early, although he knew perfectly well they wouldn't be out until the end of January. His mother had hidden his phone twice, so that he could sleep. Both times he had found it. Andrei asked him if he was nervous. His father told him no, that he was calm, and that he was checking his email for technical reasons, in case the Instituto Cervantes server had some problem. Andrei looked at his mother. His mother rolled her eyes and said he had been like that since 21 November.

Marta stayed at Ecaterina's, as the year before, in the small room overlooking the inner courtyard, the one Ecaterina now called "the Madrid room". She corrected the proofs in the mornings, at the living-room table, opposite Ecaterina, who was selecting letters for the anthology. They worked in silence for hours, each with her glasses and her red pen, and only spoke to ask each other a word. Andrei, who came by at midday to take them to lunch, said they looked like two watchmakers repairing the same watch. Ecaterina replied that no, they looked like two booksellers: one sold stories that had happened, and the other, stories that hadn't happened yet.

They celebrated Christmas Eve, as the year before, at Ana and Mihai's, in the great-grandmother's house that Ilie had renovated. This time Grandpa Gheorghe did come. Costel went to fetch him from the village on the 23rd, despite the snow, in the company truck, because he said Grandpa wasn't comfortable in an ordinary car, and because that way he could practise in the snow, in case he ran into a storm in the Pyrenees. Grandpa arrived in Bucharest sitting in the cab, in his Sunday cap, his walking stick between his knees and the oil lamp wrapped in a blanket on his lap. He said he had no intention of spending a Christmas Eve without it.

That Christmas Eve there were nineteen at the table. All of the previous year's guests were there, plus Grandpa, Andrei, and Carmen and Juan, who had come from Madrid to spend Christmas with their daughter and granddaughter. In the morning a huge box arrived from Triana by courier: polvorones, turrón de Jijona, mantecados and a bottle of sweet wine, with a card written by four hands. Doña Remedios's handwriting said: "So that Christmas Eve in Bucharest tastes a little of Triana." And underneath, Faustino's handwriting: "And so that Grandpa Gheorghe practises mus over the holidays, in case I beat him again in the summer." Inside the box there was also a pack of Spanish cards.

After dinner, Mihai put the video of the school show on the television, so that those who hadn't been there could see it too. Grandpa asked to watch it twice. The second time, when the children began to sing, he got up slowly, with his stick, stood next to the television and sang with them, in impossible Spanish, the chorus he had learned by heart from watching it eleven times: "Pero mira cómo beben los peces en el río." Rosa Elena got up and stood beside him. They sang together, the five-year-old girl and the ninety-seven-year-old man, and nobody at the table managed to sing with them, because everyone was crying or laughing, or both.

There were presents, as always. Mr Dan gave Costel an enormous steel flask, so that his coffee would stay hot from Bucharest to Valencia. Costel gave Mr Dan a diary for the following year in which he had written, on the first page, the date the C1 results came out: "end of January". And underneath: "apto". Mr Dan told him not to tempt fate. Ecaterina gave Marta an old fountain pen that had belonged to her mother, so that she could sign copies of her novel with it. Marta gave Ecaterina the first printed proof of the cover of "La librera de Triana": Faustino's back walking away, with the red beret.

Rosa Elena had a present for Grandpa. It was a small notebook she had made herself, with cardboard covers painted green, like La Lámpara's sign. Inside she had stuck photos she had taken with her camera throughout the year: the walnut tree in spring, the walnut tree in summer with the light bulbs, the snowy walnut tree in November, the oil lamp in the window, Grandpa on the porch. Under each photo she had written a word in Spanish in crooked letters. The last photo was of the snowy walnut tree, and underneath was a word that didn't exist: "nievogal". Grandpa asked her what it meant. Rosa Elena explained that it was a walnut tree so white it looked made of snow.

A week later, on New Year's Eve, Marta taught them all the tradition of the twelve grapes. She explained that in Spain, at midnight, with each of the twelve chimes of the clock at the Puerta del Sol, you had to eat a grape, so that the new year would bring good luck. That if you didn't eat them all in time, nothing terrible happened, but it was bad luck, and that was why Spaniards bought them already peeled and seedless, in case they choked. Ana had bought three kilos of grapes at the market. Mr Dan asked, like a good engineer, how many seconds there were between chimes. Marta told him three. Mr Dan said that was technically impossible.

They celebrated in the village, at Grandpa Gheorghe's, because Grandpa had said that Christmas Eve could be in Bucharest, but the new year was welcomed under the walnut tree, as always. Costel had taken him back on the 30th, and the others came on the afternoon of the 31st, in three cars. It was so cold that they had to celebrate indoors, in the big room, by the stove, with the oil lamp in the window so that it could be seen from the road. At half past eleven, Mihai connected the computer to the television, so that they could watch the chimes from the Puerta del Sol live, with an hour's difference: it would be midnight in Madrid when it was one o'clock in Romania.

So they welcomed the year twice. At midnight, Romanian time, they toasted with the sweet wine from Triana and everyone hugged, and Grandpa kissed Rosa Elena on the forehead. And at one, Madrid time, they sat in front of the television, each with a bowl of twelve grapes, peeled by Carmen all afternoon. When the chimes began, Mr Dan counted them aloud, in Spanish, so that nobody would get ahead. Marta ate them all in time, like a professional. Ana choked on the seventh. Costel ate two at once on the fourth and only one on the fifth, and said the average was correct. Juan, as always, didn't manage to finish.

At five past one, Bucharest time, Andrei got a message on his phone. It was from Begoña. It was the first time in sixteen months that Begoña had written to him outside working hours, and the first time she had written him anything that wasn't an instruction. The message said, in three lines: "Twelve grapes. Didn't choke on a single one. Happy New Year, Romanian." Andrei showed it to Marta, who laughed so hard she dropped her last grape on the floor. Lucas sent him another message five minutes later, from the stall on the Cuesta de Moyano, where he had gone to eat his grapes alone, with a candle, in Faustino's honour.

Grandpa Gheorghe didn't want grapes. He said that at his age foreign traditions had to be adapted, in case the heart didn't understand them. So, while the twelve Madrid chimes rang out, Grandpa ate twelve walnuts from his tree, shelled one by one with his own hands during the afternoon, at his own pace, slowly, without worrying about the chimes. It took him almost five minutes. When he finished, everyone applauded. Marta asked him whether he had made a wish with each walnut. Grandpa answered no, that he had made the same wish twelve times, so that nobody up there would forget it. Nobody dared ask him what it was.

Very late, when the others were asleep, scattered around the rooms of the house and in the cars, Ecaterina went out onto the porch with her coat and a candle. It had stopped snowing. The sky was so clear that all the stars were visible, and the snow shone under the moon as if it were lit from within. She sat on the bench, under the walnut tree, and took out her notebook. On the first page of the new notebook, the one for the year that had just begun, she wrote a single sentence, the first of the anthology's introduction, the one she had been looking for for weeks without finding it: "This book exists so that no letter waits longer than it has to."

Behind her the door opened. It was Grandpa, with a blanket over his shoulders and the oil lamp in his hand. He said nothing. He sat down beside her on the bench and put the lamp between them, on the snow. They stayed like that for a while, in silence, looking at the white road that went down to the village, along which, on Monday, 11 January, at five in the morning, Costel's truck would pass on its way to Valencia, with a 1980 atlas on the passenger seat and a bag of walnuts for a boy who didn't yet know he would plant a walnut tree. Then Grandpa pointed at the lamp and said in Spanish, slowly: "Para que no se apague."

Write (at least 300 words) a letter with instructions and advice for someone dear who is going on a long journey or starting something new. Explain why you give each piece of advice (purpose), what to be careful about (precaution) and what might happen (consequence).
